nameStory: The Spotted Spreadwing gets its name from two distinctive features: the dark spots that appear on its wings, and its habit of holding its wings spread wide apart when at rest. Unlike most damselflies that fold their wings back along their body, spreadwings earn their family name by keeping their wings open like tiny airplane wings even when perched.
description: The Spotted Spreadwing is a slender damselfly with a delicate build and metallic green or bronze coloration on its body. These graceful insects typically measure about 1.5 to 2 inches long with narrow, clear wings that show distinctive dark spots. Like all damselflies, they have large compound eyes that don't quite touch each other, and they flutter weakly compared to their dragonfly cousins. You'll often see them perched on vegetation near ponds and wetlands with their characteristic spread-wing posture.

idTips.label: Wing spots
idTips.description: Look for distinct dark spots on the clear wings - these spots are your best clue for identification and feel slightly raised if you gently touch them

idTips.label: Spread-wing posture
idTips.description: Wings held horizontally away from the body when resting, never folded back like most damselflies - this creates a distinctive T-shape silhouette

idTips.label: Metallic body color
idTips.description: Body appears metallic green to bronze with a subtle iridescent sheen that shifts in sunlight - feels smooth and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Separated eyes
idTips.description: Large compound eyes are clearly separated by a gap, unlike dragonflies whose eyes touch - the gap feels like a small groove if touched gently

idTips.label: Weak flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a fluttery, weak flight pattern compared to dragonflies, often staying close to vegetation and landing frequently

habitat: Spotted Spreadwings prefer quiet, vegetated ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's lowlands and foothills. They're particularly common around shallow wetlands with abundant emergent plants like cattails, sedges, and pond weeds. Look for them in areas where there's a good mix of open water and dense aquatic vegetation for egg-laying.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with males establishing territories around prime egg-laying sites. Early individuals may appear somewhat faded as they're still maturing.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you'll see the most individuals. Males patrol territories while females visit water to lay eggs. Colors are at their most vibrant and metallic during this season.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active well into fall, often until the first hard frosts. Late-season individuals may appear slightly worn with faded wing spots and duller body coloration.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - they overwinter as eggs laid in plant stems near water. The next generation will emerge the following spring.

funFact: Spotted Spreadwings have one of the most unusual mating rituals in the insect world - the male will actually guard the female for hours after mating, riding on her back like a tiny jockey while she searches for the perfect plant stem to slice open with her saw-like egg-laying organ!
confusionNotes: Spotted Spreadwings can be confused with other spreadwing species, but the wing spots are usually diagnostic. Remember: 'Spots on the wings, it's the Spotted thing!' Other spreadwings in the area typically lack these distinctive dark wing markings or have different spot patterns.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Lestes' comes from a Greek word meaning 'robber' or 'pirate,' referring to their predatory nature as both larvae and adults. Despite their delicate appearance, these are efficient hunters that will snatch small flying insects right out of the air.
compareHints: Among New England's spreadwings, the Spotted Spreadwing is one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its distinctive wing spots. The Emerald Spreadwing has a more intensely green body but lacks the wing spots, while the Northern Spreadwing tends to be larger and has different male clasper shapes (the appendages at the tip of the abdomen). The Slender Spreadwing is notably smaller and more delicate-looking overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spreadwings, the Slender Spreadwing is distinguished by its exceptionally thin body profile and pale blue face coloration.
Among New England's nine Lestes species, Swamp Spreadwings are distinguished by their strong preference for heavily vegetated wetlands and their larger, more robust build.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Amber-winged is distinguished by its wing coloration when present, though this can be subtle.
Among New England's spreadwings, the elegant spreadwing is distinguished by its bronze-brown coloration and medium size.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Northern Spreadwing is distinguished by its preference for more permanent water bodies compared to species like the Swamp Spreadwing which favors temporary pools.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Emerald Spreadwing stands out for its brilliant metallic green coloration - most others like the Swamp Spreadwing appear more bronze or brown.
Among New England spreadwings, sweetflag spreadwings are distinguished by their preference for heavily vegetated wetlands rather than open water.
